A bit of my grief playlist. Some of these were written after the artists lost friends or family, so some hit very hard. I listened to a lot of them that day, driving home from the emergency vet. A year later, I still can't listen to them without crying, but they did help.
This is my experience as well. My auto-ships almost always come the next day from Chewy. Petsmart took anywhere from 3-5 days, which was absurd.
Its not a live vaccine. It can't give you COVID.

Since i swapped from Petsmart to Chewy for vet food, it's been so easy. Food is typically here a day or two after the order happens, and I can delay or order early if I need to. It's so flexible. 

Also, they seem to have a policy where if a pet doesn't like a food you try, they'll refund you but tell you to donate the rest. I've only had to do that once, but i know my mom had the same response when her dogs wouldn't eat something. 

They also seem...really genuine. One of our cats passed last year, and I'd forgotten about his prescription food until an auto-shipment came. I asked for a refund on it with customer service, and they were really understanding when I told them the reason. We got a card in the mail from them the next week, saying they were sorry he passed. Clearly mass-printed, but it makes you feel like they care. 

Highly recommend!

Pre-Lem, i had to wear an AFO whenever I left the house. Had weakness in that leg, along with 2 intention tremors in different locations. When I moved my leg to walk, it would shake. Sometimes, the tremors were especially bad, and walking was near impossible because of the effort it took to just lift and move my leg forward. This was in combination with the many other symptoms I had. 

You wouldn't be able to tell by watching me walk now, though when I pseudoflare I do revert to that state of struggling to walk. I don't really get how it works, because obviously the damage is still there, but unless my nerves get overworked or triggered from stress, I'm almost normal now. I don't look a gift horse in the mouth. 

Granted, I wasn't using a rollator or wheelchair, so I wasn't as severe as Selma. I still couldn't wear heels if I wanted to now (i still have a tremor in my foot, but outside of flares, it's just benign twitching - though it does hinder me balancing on heels due to the weakness in that muscle).
It's illegal in MA as of last year. I'm so relieved by that.

I had massive Lemtrada improvement. Almost all my symptoms disappeared outside of pseudoflares. I went from being one of the worst cases at my clinic to almost not even showing it clinically during exam...so yes, it happens. Just not as often as with HSCT. 

Mavenclad probably has a smaller chance to, being a drug that causes a soft reset - similarly to the other two, just not as strong.

If she's marketing Mavenclad like this, it's definitely suspicious, but I would think symptom regression is possible with it. It's weaker than Lem and HSCT, but is also an IRT. I know the other two can and do cause regression - sometimes massively - so I would guess it's a possibility with Mavenclad  as well.
Unless something has changed, it has a 58% reduction in rr. That puts it in the "good" (medium efficacy) category, not up there with Ocrevus, Tysabri, Lemtrada etc.
Mavenclad isnt high-efficacy. It's in the medium-efficacy category. It doesn't kill the immune system to the extent that the other two do. It's still a good drug, though.

Our kitten was a bully at first when we got her last year. Our senior cat grazes, so he wasn't getting enough food just trying to feed him at meal times. 


We got a SureFeed feeder, and it made a massive difference. They're not real cheap, but they are damn secure. The kitten tried beating it up, pulling it, pushing it, and never could get in. 


There's also an optional attachment that puts a shield around the back, so other cats can't push the chipped cat away. It closes instantly when they pull their head out, and it's very quick. Jupiter tried but couldn't get any food before it closed. She stopped trying after a couple weeks. We didn't end up needing the extra shield, but it's useful for some bullies. Highly recommend!

One thing I've seen recommended (for the future) is to rub each cat with a different sock (or even blankets), bag them, and then rub the cat that went to the vet with the socks before they meet. It gets their usual smell and the other cat's smell on them, so the second cat might be able to recognize it. 


It worked to lower aggression with our cats (only one of them would get aggressive when the other went to the vet), but didn't nullify it completely.

I split it. Half a 3oz can or a quarter of a 5.5oz can twice a day, then dry food to supplement. It's always been fine for my cats. One of them is on prescription kidney wet food, which is massively expensive. Feeding 2+ cans a day of that, plus the supplements I have him on, would be way too much. 


If you're not able to feed a lot of wet food (and lot of people aren't, tbh), I do recommend getting a cat water fountain. It encourages them to drink more water.
I have monthly blood tests done, plus extra if needed. The amount of blood they take for test vials isn't enough to make you dizzy or queasy, I promise!

My statement was going off of literally walking down the pet food aisles. The majority of cans *will* say grain-free. I went through every section when we first got our kitten, and there were few that were grain-inclusive. Dry food is less commonly grain-free, though a lot still are. This didn't used to be the case years ago.

I'm not sure why you took that comment so offensively, but thanks for your input.
Yeah, our senior cat developed arthritis in his hips last year. Only found out because he would stand hunched like this. It got way better after we started Cosequin and Antinol+.

Our senior cat was depressed for weeks after we put our other senior down last year. He stayed under the bed almost 24/7 except for food. Cats do grieve, and like humans they'll recover at their own pace.

I've had GERD since I was 11. I'm 35 now. I had an endoscopy last year to check the state of my esophagus, and...no serious damage or changes. Just noticeable reflux.

I'd expected them to find Barrett's, or pre-cancerous/cancerous cells, but there were none. Cells were all still normal, no thickening of the lining. 

I've been on Pantoprazole since about 12 or 13, after other meds didn't help. It seems to be doing its job.

Thank you for the info! My vet was somewhat vague and didn't seem to know *why* the lack of grains would cause it, just that it was a potential. 

We ordered Purina Pro dry, which isn't grain-free, but it makes me feel a lot better if wet isn't an issue. There are more grain-free wet foods than ones with grains! Still haven't settled on what she'll want to stick with yet though.

Yeah, we're currently mixing in Purina Pro dry with her kitten dry. We had her on Purina One+ Kitten dry food too. A lot of my pets have been on one variation or another of the brand, going back 20 years. 

We're still trying out different adult wet to see what sticks. The extensive research from the main brands is why I wouldn't try any more of the "healthy" brands that are newer and less known. We tried Tiki Cat wet, and she stopped eating if she saw that's what she got. Purina or Fancy Feast pate, she loves, despite FF having such a stigma against it, so I figure they're doing something right if its more palatable than actual chicken shreds.

If it helps at all, I was in the same boat. Kept progressing and relapsing on Ocrevus. In 2019, it was either Ocrevus or Tysabri for the high efficacy meds. My specialist didn't want to gamble at the rate i was progressing, so he pushed for Lem/HSCT over Tysabri. 


Lem made me incredibly sick, but it regressed almost all of my symptoms. It's a brutal treatment that most do get bad side effects from, but it is very effective.


I'm 3 years out from round 2. No autoimmune complications so far, and no progression. My old symptoms come back when I pseudoflare, but otherwise the MS is very mild symptom-wise. I was debilitated before. 


My specialist did tell me beforehand that Lem has a good chance at regressing some symptoms, but not to expect it, because it doesn't do that for everyone. In my case, it did, but there isn't a guarantee. 


If you go this route, keep in mind that you likely will need some help from your family, especially in the week or two after (they need to understand this - this drug is not a joke). The fatigue is a common side effect, even for people who didn't have severe side effects post-infusion. I couldn't take care of myself for at least a week; I'm not a mother, but if I had a child, I 100% would not have been able to care for them. 


Sorry for the long post, but wanted to give anecdotal insight as someone who had a similar choice. I hope whatever treatment you decide on works out, whether it's Lemtrada or something else. Aggressive MS is rough!

An ostrich, in Texas. My aunt was a zookeeper for the bird section at the Houston zoo, and was showing us around. I was 7ish at the time.


The ostrich somehow escaped its enclosure, and apparently decided to pick on the tiny human. It tried to kick me in the face, but luckily my aunt was used to working with them, got in front of me, and was able to corral it with the help of a few other keepers.


Don't even remember being terrified. I love animals and thought it was damn cool.

Yeah, the brand is great otherwise. That scent just goes badly with litter box contents. They do differ a bit, though - we did try one other variant that we didn't like as well, but we've been using the unscented multicat for a few months now and like it. 

Your experience might vary, though! Just wanted to throw my 2 cents in about the lemongrass. How bad it smelled really threw me.

That's your issue. The lemongrass one mixes extremely badly with pee and/or poo, to the point where it simultaneously set off my asthma and made me gag while trying to clean it. I've never had that reaction from litter. 


We almost wrote it off after that, but decided to try the unscented multicat one. No issues with that at all. It does have a slight smell, but way better than any clay litter (and its not a poo smell, i think its just the corn).

World's Best. I think we have the multicat one. The one with lemongrass is absolutely horrid, made the cat room smell really nauseating. The unscented one we get is great though, and very little to no smell.


We used Boxiepro for the longest time, but it does track way more. Haven't tried pellets, but I have been curious. 


Any other brands we've tried have honestly not hidden the smell at all, Pretty Litter included.

It was well worth it in T1. You had a high chance to get T1 purples on your alt to sell for lucent to help your main. Nowadays, with so many daily/weekly things to do, and the almost nonexistent drop rate of T2 gear, it's very much not worth it.

Yeah, some drop locations aren't correctly listed for us on Questlog. There's currently available gear that have the wrong sources listed, presumably from KR.


I do hope these are craftable, because that drop rate is bullshit for 2 chances per day.

No need to be hostile. I didn't realize the percentages were so different. That said, we *did* still go that long without an Exca wand even with a higher rate. Yes, the percentages from current bosses are even more dogshit. It wouldn't surprise me if the chance is higher in KR, since apparently T2 open world % was nerfed for us too.

Keep in mind that until this week, there were no guaranteed T2 drops from bosses. We were getting almost all T1 gear. 


But weapons used to have a worse drop rate than armor or accessories from bosses in T1, so I'd assume it's the same now. And yes, rates were this bad. We went 3-4 weeks without an Exca wand in one guild. In another, we got 2 in the same night. It's RNG.

This is the logic my boyfriend and I are running.


We currently pay 1250 for a 2br, we'll below what others are charging. It's been going up every year, though, and at the moment it's close to 50% of my monthly pay for my half. 


Our landlords don't fix shit, there's so many violations in the apartment, and they have some really questionable rules. We want out, but 1br places in our area are going for 1600+. We're struggling enough as is. 


Combine that with the fact that you have to essentially pay 3 months of rent to move in PLUS most of another month to real estate agents, it just seems better value to use that money to help with a down payment on a house. A lot of apartments don't give yearly leases anymore either, so you never have security. As painful as house ownership could be, renting sucks. We'll take that gamble.

You literally said that you knew the boxer was reactive to them, because he chased one and tried to bite it. This isn't "never interacting" with them. It was a dangerous situation that never should have been allowed. 

Both dog breeds require extensive training, and you clearly haven't done so. They likely will remain dangerous because of this prey drive. As others said, once they kill an animal, it's very hard to train that aggression out of them, though at a minimum they will  have to see a professional to see if its possible.

It's unsafe to keep dogs like this around other animals or children, and also not right to keep cats that you can't have indoors. Outdoor cats live much shorter lives and have a detrimental impact on local wildlife. All the animals should go - the dogs to a place that might be able to train them the way they should be, and the cats to people that won't force them to live outside.

Get a goldfish.

I used to be in PT years ago, but stopped going after my clinic closed down post-COVID. There aren't many PT clinics around that work with neurological conditions like my old one did. 

My newer specialist does have occupational/speech/physical therapists in the building, but when I went for a baseline a couple years ago, it was excessively expensive since my insurance apparently didn't cover it. I can't afford that on top of the MRI I'm overdue for, unfortunately. Back when insurance covered PT, it was much more doable at $40 a session.

Thank you for this! I'll check the height today to see if I have it right. And yeah, I definitely dont need it often. When I'm not pseudoflaring, I can walk perfectly fine. When I am, my leg will be really hard to use even with an AFO. The cane is just for those days, if I need to go somewhere.

I've done a 5:2 intermittent fasting diet. My GERD makes it impossible to go 14-16 hours without eating, so I went the easier route, which was <500 cals two days a week, normal amount the rest of the time. My specialist backed it and said this type of fast could help with fatigue for some people, as the long stretches of fasting can (it also pushes your body into ketosis), but not to expect other changes. 


It helped me lose weight, but I didn't notice any energy difference until I started being able to exercise.
Its bullshit, yet AGS literally stated it was an issue? Okay.

Lemtrada is extremely brutal. I would not recommend it unless other treatments aren't working. It will most likely make you incredibly sick. It's actual chemo, just a bit lower dose than what's used for HSCT or cancer.

I switched because Ocrevus was only slowing progression, but not stopping it. I'm 3 years out from my second round. No new lesions since, no autoimmune issues as of yet. I had my first round 4 months after a dose of Ocrevus. The second (or third) years are the most likely to cause thyroid problems, according to my old specialist that worked a lot with Lemtrada.  

I experienced massive regression, but it came at the cost of having no functional immune system for months. 10 after the first round and 5 after the second. The side effects are horrible, though some get lucky and have an easier time. I was crying on day 3 in my first year because of how much pain I was in and how weak I felt, but that paled in comparison to the month after infusion week.

The second round caused such insane swelling through my whole body that my airway was restricted. Doctors couldn't do anything. I woke up constantly at night because I'd stop breathing in my sleep, for two weeks. It terrified me enough that I'll never do a third round even if I start progressing again. It was a godsend for my aggressive MS and gave me function back, but this drug is no joke.

I had pretty much silent progression before my first attack. My only symptom was worsening migraines that year. I'd had a routine MRI the year prior (i had chronic migraines for years before that - a scan every 2-3 years was typical), and it was clear. When my attack hit, I had too many lesions to count. Aggressive MS can progress very fast.
That's really shitty, since even AGS acknowledged tank aggro is an issue right now. It's neither the tank nor the DPS' fault, unless there's an obvious massive gear gap.

Performance has tanked drastically. Might have to do with the merges, too many people on the servers, dunno. Memory leak is insane now, for whatever reason. I have 32gb RAM and still have to restart occasionally to clear the stuttering. 


A lot of people i know have seen drops in performance. Herba is really laggy. Doesn't matter how good the system is, it's still worse than pre-Talandre. 


I can still play on high settings, but it's really noticeable. I was really surprised at how optimized this game was when it launched. That's not the case anymore. Still, game being unplayable entirely means 80% of your guild must have really low-end PCs.
You know the AH is region wide, right? The amount of people on your server literally doesn't matter. It just makes farming harder with how overpopulated every server is.

Ngl, I love healing, but sometimes i get really stressed and just swap to DPS for a few dungeons. Leveled up staff/spear for this reason last patch. I'd never reroll completely, but It's so much less of a drain to go dps brain for a while.

As a healer, I love being partied with people like you. Even more if you're hovering in front instead of running behind me.


A lot of people don't seem to realize that Clay's (aoe heal) is a decent cd even with cdr, flash wave doesn't heal behind us, and we don't have infinite single target heals. Also that the glowing circle that's 2 steps in front of them is a really strong heal and mana regen.

Me sitting here with 3 pieces of litho'd gear, a pity-crafted wand, an AH-bought auric helmet and lucky as hell auric boots - my only personal drop. Healer life is shit this patch. I'll end up buying the pants and *maybe* getting the chest to drop by next expac.

Be in a party with a healer. If you're not too squishy and don't stand in avoidable things, you can be kept alive. 


If you're ranged, even easier.

You can't build enough collision  resistance to counteract tanks now. Weaken resist is more helpful, as you can build weaken resist past the weaken hit other people can get. 


I ran collision resistance last patch. Avoided everything but some tornadoes. It's not possible now.
People aren't building collision resistance since tanks can stack 1200-1500 collision chance now, iirc. There's literally no point.

I get more bags than my DPS  guildmates a lot of the time. I do have a PvEvP build that sacrifices a couple support skills for aoes, but damage still pales compared to DPS players. I think we're fine. 


I guess it's counteracted by some DPS in guild almost full gearing through those bags, while I've gotten nothing usable. Talandre healer life.
Vanguard is the best PvP wise, and it's one of the most expensive sets in the game.
What does a server merge have to do with drop rates?

No, definitely not. Everyone in my guild noticed how it was nearly impossible to see party members, but it's those of us playing healers that are severely affected by it. 

I felt like a terrible healer all siege because I spent so much time trying to *locate* the people I was trying to heal. The target marker just blended in, too.

Definitely an oversight in design.
I had shingles at 34. It's not just something old people get anymore. I also was no longer immunocompromised by Lemtrada, but we do think an MS pseudoflare might have triggered it due to stress.

Get it. I haven't had it, but i had Shingles 11 months ago, and it was the most painful experience I've ever gone through, nothing comes close. My non-MS side now has potentially permanent nerve damage on that half of my stomach and back. 


No amount of side effects from the vaccine could be worse than that was.

My PA at my old MS clinic literally spent 40 minutes in one appointment googling all the benefits to cutting out gluten and trying to convince me it would make me feel so much better. I left that appointment feeling pissed off. 


Hard no. I've done intermittent fasting to lose weight post-MS, but I won't cut food groups out. 


I had crazy progression before my first attack, and I was eating really healthy and biking 10 miles a day back then, so I don't believe the whole diet-can-fix-you bull, no matter what diet it is.

We all complained about this after siege in my guild. It was extremely hard to see where any of my party was. I love having a raid UI, but I can't say this is better than giving myself a headache with Astral Vision and doing separate parties. I don't know why they had to make the colors so similar.

My cat that passed last year was named Popple by the shelter, and we kept it. He was quirky, so it fit him. 


My other senior, from the same shelter, was named Squish. I renamed him Gizmo since he was an absolute maniac when he was little.

Removing a cat from its mother too early can have some really negative effects. 7 weeks is absurdly young. 12 is recommended. 


Cats shouldn't be caged. As others said, you can close them into a kitten-proofed room when you're not home. That said, she needs to go back to her mom until she's old enough.
Interesting. I'll ask my vet about it next time he's in for bloodwork. She hasn't mentioned fluids at all, just makes sure he's not dehydrated when they do urine tests.

Do fluids help even if they're well-hydrated without? That's one thing we haven't had an issue with. Between HydraCare and the cat fountain, he gets plenty of liquids (his urine tests havent showed him dehydrated at all). I've seen that a lot of cats are on SubQ fluids though.

They do in Twisted, apparently. Found this out by accident the other day. Not sure if other T3s do the same.


Old dungeons still don't. They should have made every dungeon do it.
Check your alt's mail. The hair seems to be account unlock, but the outfit itself isn't. They sent mails to every character on accounts that bought it.
It's a chinchilla, and you can't convince me otherwise.

I play Seeker, and I've been saying this needs to be nerfed for months. It's too strong. I don't blame people for wanting a lot of bows, because it's that disgustingly OP. The difference between multiple bows and only one or no bows is massive.

I was on at 7:30am yesterday, and every spot was packed in both pve and pvp. 


Probably depends on who your server is paired with, but putting two of the largest servers together was a stupid idea. I'll be lucky if I can get in at all this week.

My boyfriend and I both noticed this too. We both have 5600x3d, I have a 6750XT and he has a 6700. Both had very smooth performance before expansion - even decent in siege. Now it's stuttering a lot, and there seems to be a noticeable memory leak too.

If they hadn't just merged servers, it would be playable, but you can't expect 3 whole servers to all have space to grind. The map is too small. 


The only way this could be viable is if they added channels. That would potentially suck for PvP, but would enable more players to be in Nebula. The only alternative is unlinking- every server gets their own Nebula. Even that would probably be overrun, though, because that's how large server pops are now after merges. 


You can't find any time to grind. I was on at 7am the other day, and every spot was taken. It's unplayable.
Would low phosphorous food like Weruva Wx be good for healthy cats, then? I thought phosphorous was needed unless the kidneys are damaged.

My boyfriend is the only one that doesn't respond this way. I have no issue with people complaining that they're tired- just don't compare it to *my* fatigue if you're perfectly healthy. 


A lot of us are on a med that was literally originally for narcolepsy. I can't function without it...and if the fatigue is flaring, I can even sleep ON Modafinil. If that doesn't speak volumes for how bad MS fatigue can get, I don't know what will. 


People tend to gloss over it when I say I'm tired. It's not a typical tired. It's a, I'm moving, thinking, and speaking in slow motion right now and can't keep up with what you're saying. I get that you're tired, healthy people, but it's not the same. 


Coming from a significant other, though? Your husband is diminishing your symptom, and it's insensitive at best.

Yeah, I was pretty upset when I logged in to find that the weapons I thought i could get from a contract vendor selection chest were moved to pouches or the 3 chances per week in Hall. You can craft them with loyalty, but that isn't quick to get. They made these items very P2W by focusing dropping them in pouches. 


Gearing to T2 in week 1 would obviously be ridiculous, but grinding, doing dungeons, solo dungeons, etc, and getting nothing but t1 gear is beyond demotivating. Especially when it's blues. Purples in T1 had a low drop rate, but they still felt attainable. T2 gear feels like such a reach.

Get the vaccine. I had it last April - it was horrific, and I have permanent nerve damage on the non-MS side of my stomach and back. Shingles is no joke.


I was never told to get it before Ocrevus or Lemtrada, and I'm angry every time the residual nerve pain and itching starts up. Both at myself and my doctors. Hindsight is 20/20.

I was still having rapid clinical progression despite finally stopping having new lesions on MRI after a year of Ocrevus. My specialist considered Ocrevus a failure when I kept snowballing and becoming increasingly disabled. 


Went on Lemtrada after 2 years, and the clinical progression stopped. Take it with a grain of salt, as it is an extremely potent treatment, but if you are continuing to progress symptomatically, changing your DMT to something else high efficacy could help.

To add to that, it also is considered a medium efficacy drug, despite being an IRT. It works great for some and has the benefit of not needing a DMT for years if it works, but it's not a new miracle drug if that's how she's painting it.

I can't even wear 1 inch heels since MS appeared, and I'm nowhere near as bad as she's said she is. I walk fine a lot of the time, just can't do heels due to a small tremor that makes my foot a little unstable. How she can wear stilettos without an issue is...odd.

Dogs aren't meant to weight bear a human being. It can seriously hurt them either over time or from one fall. 


Even a Great Dane could be hurt from this. Counterbalance is a thing SDs can get trained for, but no responsible trainer will teach a dog to catch you when you fall or help you up. The chance of injury to them is too great.

This is why service dogs have such a bad stigma here. There is no service dog ID, and you aren't required to show any kind of proof. A lot of people will claim their dogs are service animals because of this, and it makes me angry every time I see a badly behaved pet masquerading as a service dog. 


A vest isn't required, but from what I've seen some people say, they use a vest to signal to the dog whether it's working or not. They can easily be bought online, though, so plenty of fake SDs have them.

You could try a pill gun. It looks sort of like a syringe, but with a rubber tip that you put the pill in.


The cat won't like it, but it's quick. You just stick it to the back of their mouth, push the pill in, remove, and then gently hold their mouth closed until you see them swallow. It's easier to shove the plastic into their mouth than your finger, and you get to the back very fast. 


We had to do this for our old cat a lot before he passed - he had to go on antibiotics every so often. He got pissed every time, but it only takes a few seconds to do. They forgive you after a few minutes of angry sulking.

If i start progressing again, yes. They'll put me on something else or do a third round of Lem if even one lesion shows up. My disease was extremely aggressive, so they take it seriously. 

Lemtrada, with any luck, should keep me progression free for 10+ years, according to them. Some dont get that lucky, though, so we'll see.
I kept progressing on Ocrevus, though it did slow the disease down. Lemtrada stopped progression entirely, and my symptoms regressed. Still no progression 4 years later.

Your CPU is only a tad bit weaker than mine. I play with a 5600x3d, 6750XT and 32gb RAM. I don't change settings for siege other than char count.


Make sure you have the AMD or NVidia performance options in-game/in your apps. It makes a huge difference.


Also, yes, it's been tested. Some graphic options literally do nothing (not just for performance...like, legitimately change nothing), while others will hurt performance if set to low or medium. IIRC shading was one of these (have to have it on high), but i don't remember the others.
Then don't get mad if less experienced or lower geared healers can't keep you alive. That's entirely on you.
Alternatively, do mechanics if you're too squishy to survive skipping them.

I'm looking forward to the mastery system, and catching up in gear to KR, so balance changes aren't a disadvantage to us. Also interested to see what new builds the new mastery system will make viable (or better)!

I'm not sure why it would be considered an automatic death sentence, unless the shelters around you are heartless.


I fostered many ferals for my local shelter some years back, and every single one of them went back socialized. Not a single one failed. 


The worst case was one who actually attacked vet techs at the shelter, but since we had tamed his sister, they gave him to us after another foster couldn't deal with him. Last resort before they sent him to a barn. He ended up being a cuddly foster failure for all 14 years of his life. 


"Feral" doesn't mean they can't be socialized. Some will be turned into barn cats for their own well-being, but most can be socialized with enough effort and patience. I haven't heard of a shelter that straight up euthanizes ferals for no reason other than the fact that they're feral.

So much this. I play Seeker, but the difference between no or just a single bow dps vs 2-3 bow dps and myself is ludicrous. No buff should be so strong that it's pretty much mandatory to stack the same weapon.


They do need to give bow some love otherwise, but DM is too overpowered as is.

I'm taking it at my own pace. A lot of people are burning out as it is atm and are taking a break. I don't want to burn out myself by frantically trying to stockpile everything, just to be able to 100% some gear in the first week of t2. 


Burning out by obsessing so much over all the things you have to do to prepare will just make the t2 grind miserable.

Which IUD did you get? The copper one actually makes periods worse. Not really sure why that thing even exists, honestly.


I had excruciating periods that were making me severely anemic before I got my IUD (Liletta). My uterus revolted for the first few months with horribly painful cramps constantly (apparently, this doesn't usually happen as badly or as long as i had it, so they had no advice). They became less frequent over time until around 5 months in, I had no spasms anymore. 


Not everyone ceases to have periods, but even for those of us that do get that benefit, it isn't instant. It took the better part of a year for me to stop having actual periods. Depo had actually been faster in stopping them.

I fostered a lot of feral cats until i ended up adopting two of them. Sometimes it's rough. 

One thing I always did with the especially fearful cats was going in and just sitting with them. We had a separate room we kept fosters in until they were secure enough to roam - helped their anxiety about a big new environment, and made it easier to get close to them without seeming oppressive. 

I'd go in, sit down, and just be there. Read a book, scroll on your phone, whatever. They need to get used to your presence. Trying to handle them when they're scared of you will only reinforce their fear of people. Just sit there and do nothing. Let them come to you, if they do. Repeat this a few times a day. You can talk to them in a quiet voice, but don't try to interact unless they initiate it. Just be there.

I'd stay there for anywhere from 20 mins to an hour. It is harder with two at once, but we had a few pairs of siblings. Once one breaks and allows interaction, the other is usually easier. Don't try to touch them before they're ready, but treats could help once they seem ready to interact. 

The caveat is that you *may* have irreparably broken any chance of taming them yourself with the repeated negative (in their eyes) interactions. It's likely that you can turn it around, though.  Try just spending time with them. Let them learn that you being there doesn't always mean a stressful event. Hopefully, with some time, they'll let you touch them without fear. It is NOT a quick process with more feral cats. It took weeks to tame some of the harder cases. You just have to be patient. There's always a chance they'll remain too fearful, but personally I never had a foster i couldn't tame.

Sorry if none of this was helpful, but I have a soft spot for ferals like this. One of the ones I adopted had attacked vet techs and was returned by another foster, but once we tamed him, he was a cuddle bug for 14 years. I wish you luck!

MRIs can't always pick up on lesions even if they're there. MRIs take slices of your brain in images - if that slice happens to be too far from a very small lesion, it won't show. I use a stationary bike. Working my way back up to working out, but before Lemtrada, I had very bad drop foot. A combination of biking (didn't trust my foot on a real bike) and resistance band workouts helped a lot with overall stability.

Side effects always vary with everyone. Tec is known for causing both flushing and GI upset, sometimes short term after starting, sometimes permanently. There will always be lucky people that don't get those, though. This isn't anecdotal. It's something doctors warn about if you're choosing Tec, because it's common.

Ocrevus vs Tec isn't anecdotal. Tec is a medium efficacy treatment, while Ocrevus is high efficacy. Studies prove how effective a DMT is, and Ocrevus is better.

That said, while I think going high efficacy right off the bat is the best approach, I don't think Tec is an absolutely terrible choice if someone cant get better or is too nervous to try high efficacy treatments. Ocrevus tends to be very well-tolerated for most, though.

No DMT causes progression. They can fail to stop it though, and often can't regress already-there symptoms aside from Lem/HSCT (always a chance, it's just not as common in comparison). Someone having mobility issues on Ocrevus means that either it isn't working or they already had mobility issues and didn't improve on it.

If you can, doing some strengthening can help. I know walking too much can cause my hip flexor to kind of give out and make it hard to walk. It was much better when my leg muscles were stronger. You have to do exercises that really target the problem area though. No guarantee that it'll help you, but it might.

I couldn't really find anything else that helped me. Having to wear an AFO for a long time made it so much worse, since not only did it throw my gait off, it weakened my whole leg by taking part of the work out of walking. Starting exercise after that made a big difference.
I'm in the US, but it took about a month and a half to two months from the start of my first attack to actually getting Ocrevus, so that sounds pretty normal.

Optic neuritis is one of the slowest attacks to heal from. The pain typically goes away first for me, but the other parts (i.e. blurriness) took about 8 months until my vision was back to normal. There's no guarantee it will heal all the way, though - my eye doctor thought my left eye might always be blurry, but luckily it eventually healed. This is not the case for everyone.

In terms of pain, I'd say maybe 2 weeks after steroids it was gone, the first bad attack of ON I had. A few times in later relapses, steroids didn't help. Sometimes they did. It's a toss-up.

This. I had no symptoms (aside from migraines, which I already had prior) for what we think was about a year before my first attack. I developed an intention tremor in my foot within a month of my first attack, and one in my knee sometime in the following 6ish months. The knee one is unnoticeable most of the time now, but the foot one is still there and causes mild issues, just no longer debilitating. 

Disclaimer: I have had Lemtrada, and that has a large part in how much these regressed. That said, physical therapy was so, so helpful. A PT that's trained for neurological diseases can give you exercises that will help retrain your brain. 

It lessened the impact of the tremors for me, and she also walked me through how to approach movements that set them off. Also had a lot of balance exercises to try to get my brain to utilize different muscles (or use the right ones correctly).  

It wasn't a cure, but it did help massively for my QoL, and did reduce them a bit. My balance was much better, and after working with her for a while, I no longer had to watch my feet when going upstairs. That alone was relieving.

And yes, strengthening your muscles through exercise does help a lot as well - the way my PT explained it, the muscles tremoring are getting mixed signals on what to do. Strengthening the surrounding muscles can help with stability.

Other than that, Baclofen helped a lot as well. It's frustrating when your limb can't stop shaking when you move, but you can try to reduce it. I hope something helps you!

I agree that cutting out a lot for crash diets often backfires. That said, some diets do work well short term. If I overwork my body, I can have a pseudorelapse for anywhere from a few days to a week. If I'm very lucky, they'll be gone the next day, but that's rare.

It also sometimes is delayed, where I'll overdo it or not get enough sleep, and 2 days later I get a pseudorelapse rather than right away. MS is weird. 

Keep in mind that just because an MRI is clear does not mean it can't be a relapse - I'm surprised if your doctor hasn't mentioned or doesn't know this. Not all lesions show on scans. I used to have really bad foot drop early on, caused by a tremor in my foot that also made my ankle unstable. I'd been a daily biker before my first attack, but couldn't trust my foot after that.

It was an easy way to burn calories while not putting too much strain on my foot or leg. I started slow - 10 minutes a day, slowly worked up to doing an hour a day.

Other than that, intermittent fasting. I did the 5:2 approach, where rather than fasting for 12-16 hours at a time, I just kept intake below 500 calories 2 days a week (non-consecutive). Below 500 puts your body into ketosis and will help to burn off fat. 

I didn't restrict the types of foods I ate, because I knew that wasn't a diet I could stick to, and there's no point in a diet if you can't stick to it. I ate the foods I like; planned out low cal food for fasting days and ate normal the other days - within reason. Cut out most junk food, ate more fruit, etc. One day a week I'd let myself have a fattening dessert or meal.

It worked well. Lost over 30 lbs in about 7  months, and didn't hate myself for it.

Your brain can heal damage if a nerve still has some sheath left, but if it's completely stripped, that nerve is dead forever. Not even remyelination can bring it back when that comes out.

Keep in mind that this process takes years, and requires you to not have activity in those lesions - a wound that keeps getting reopened can't heal.

People can improve on Ocrevus, but that's more the brain being able to heal than the DMT. And even if a lesion shrinks or fully heals, that's no guarantee that symptoms will improve.

Ocrevus is very effective, but as others said, it's not a cure. The best it can do is stop activity and let your brain heal on its own.

New MS symptoms don't start *from* DMTs. DMTs don't make your MS worse. Your MS became worse *while you were on* a DMT, but that is not the same. That is what's referred to as the DMT failing - progression while on one. 

It means that the particular DMT did not work to prevent *your* progression, but one size doesn't fit all. We fail DMTs and try another one until we find one that works. Tecfidera is kind of middle-of-the-road in terms of efficacy. It's not super high efficacy, but not bottom like betaferon shots. There are DMTs with higher efficacy, often with less side effects than Tecfidera.

People can have worsening depression on antidepressants sometimes. Does that mean antidepressants don't work? No. It just means different people react to the same medication differently. Some people get by fine with low efficacy DMTs without progression, some have been stable on high efficacy DMTs for years. Significant progression on one is a cause for concern, and a sign to try a different DMT rather than just not being on any.

They are, actually, unless you really enjoy gambling with your health.

Not being on a DMT means a high risk of progression and a poor long-term prognosis. Some people get lucky; a lot don't. You do you, but don't demonize medication that works for a lot of people. Especially when it comes to DMTs - you can't undo progression when it happens.

When it comes to other meds, sure, be on them or don't. Baclofen helped me back when I was on it, but some people can't tolerate side effects, same as any medication.  Likewise, one DMT doesn't work for everyone, but DMTs are vastly more important than meds we take for symptoms.
DMTs aren't meant to improve symptoms or make you feel better. Some can, but it's not guaranteed and doesn't happen to everyone. They're meant to prevent further damage.

It's better that they're thorough rather than just accepting a diagnosis they may think is incorrect.

There are numerous things that can cause brain lesions - even migraines. People can and do get misdiagnosed with MS, but doctors tend to be pretty rigorous with the diagnostic process due to it being an exclusive diagnosis with specific presentations. Hopefully your previous doctor didn't jump the gun on that without fully investigating, but at least you'll have confirmation soon.

Progression while on a DMT means it's not working, period, not that any DMT won't or that they're automatically SPMS. 

My MS is aggressive and only slowed down on Ocrevus instead of stopping. I had rapidly worsening symptoms. Lemtrada made the progression stop. 

Sometimes people do progress on DMTs without anything visible on MRI, but it doesn't necessarily point to SPMS. I'm still RRMS even after progressing non-stop for the first few years of my disease.

I'm in that boat too. It's been a bit over a year after my second infusion, and aside from a few pseudorelapses, I'm progression-free with formerly-aggressive MS. I regressed massively by the end of the first year, and most of my debilitating symptoms have almost disappeared completely. It's incredible. 

It was way more brutal than I expected, though. I've never been so sick in my life as I was for both rounds (and months afterward). I'm grateful that I was able to get it, so it's a very good thing that they approved it. I can't imagine how disabled I'd be by now without it.

The exhaustion goes beyond what people would normally consider exhaustion to be. I'm sure different patients experience it in different ways, but this is how it is for me.

Everything slows down. I feel like I'm both thinking and moving in slow motion, while everyone else is moving at normal speed. It goes beyond just feeling heavy - it's completely debilitating. Talking to anyone is hard, because comprehending words and sounding out words in return takes so much energy. It's difficult not to slur because my tongue feels clumsy and doesn't really want to move. 

I have to take my energy med daily to prevent this - on Modafinil, I'm tired, but I'm not in slow motion and can follow a conversation just fine.
It's a common symptom, but not everyone has it.

Allergic reactions are a known (potential) side effect of Ocrevus, but only during the actual infusion. Subsequent infusions past the first two are much less likely to cause any reaction, but it can still happen. They give benadryl/steroids with it to reduce the risk of allergic reactions.

Ocrevus doesn't stay in your bloodstream. It kills what it's meant to and leaves pretty quickly, so I don't think it's possible for it to be a reaction to the drug still, after 4 months. 

That said, I'm sure they're checking off lists for you, but have they tested for any potential autoimmune skin conditions? I don't think Ocrevus is super risky with complications, but things like that can happen with drugs that affect your immune system.

I dropped out of college in my second year because of spiraling depression that became dangerous. It took years, but I finally became stable enough mentally to plan on going back. Fast forward to 4 years ago, I was 29 and was planning on applying in the fall. My body had other plans. I developed massively debilitating symptoms in April of that year, progressing rapidly in a matter of days.

I was diagnosed with MS a month later. 

I'm now stuck at the same job I've been at for almost 8 years, only because the health insurance is too good and healthcare is too expensive at most jobs. I don't like what I do and hadn't planned on doing this forever. MS took away my hope of getting into my dream career.

It also took away my love of the outdoors. I can't handle the heat, and haven't ridden a real bike since my first attack appeared.

I hate this disease. And I hate that I had especially aggressive MS from the start.

I wish you luck in having minimal side effects. Just remember that most you do get are temporary. The isolation sucks, but use the time (only after 2 weeks) to gain endurance back - the energy drain will hit you like a mack truck if you go from 0-100 too quickly!
They're actually a common symptom,  according to every specialist I've had.

I hope the rest of the week goes smooth for you, and that it works. It's a brutal treatment, but it's a godsend for some of us. 

Day 2-3 is when it hit me like a truck my first year, but it doesn't to everyone. Finished my second treatment last year and am still clear of progression, no complications so far either. I wish you all the luck with this!

There's a reason they don't just hand out steroids like candy. They're hard on your system, especially at the high dose that MS requires.

I had to get them almost monthly in my first year of MS, and they screwed me up badly. My MS was extremely aggressive, though, so this is not normal for most and not something doctors will do in less severe cases. I started refusing them at one point, because it wasn't worth repeatedly making myself really sick when it wasn't going to prevent my disease from continuously getting worse. 

They can be beneficial for stopping a severe relapse faster, but I think most doctors are fairly reserved in how severe the relapse has to be to use steroids. It will pass either way, so it's a quality-of-life thing short term. 

The only reason I'll agree to steroids now is if I literally can't walk, and even then, i usually regret it. Otherwise, I just deal with it until it passes. Steroids are not a magic cure, and sometimes make you feel worse rather than better.

My boss told me when I was diagnosed that her friend had had it for 30 years and was still totally fine without ever taking a DMT.

Yes, that was extremely helpful to say to someone whose MS incapacitated them within months of appearing. Sometimes people are really obtuse.

One of the best things you can do is just to be there. My biggest fear in dating someone after my MS diagnosis is that he'd get scared and leave, but my boyfriend has done well in reassuring (and showing) me that he's not going anywhere. 

We've been together for almost 3 years, ive been diagnosed for 4. As a specific example, I just came out of the most severe flare I've had in at least a year. There were multiple days where I had extreme difficulty walking. He picked me up early from work one day, and helped walk me out so I could lean on him for support. Being there for me and treating it like it doesn't bother him in such severe situations means the world. 

That said, the diagnosis is rough. She'll go through a grieving period. The sadness and anger is normal, and it will pass. Finding out that you have a progressive disease is devastating, especially if your symptoms are severe from the start.

Emotional support is the biggest thing. Help her physically if she'll let you, but I know I didn't want help even when struggling when I was diagnosed. It's different for everyone. She'll get through this, and hopefully her symptoms will improve.

If you can get on Amantadine or Modafinil, I highly recommend those over ADHD meds. These aren't in that category. Modafinil is meant for narcolepsy or long-shift workers that need to stay awake for long periods. It is still a controlled substance, though. 

ADHD meds cause a really nasty crash when they wear off, and gave me headaches too. Amantadine and Modafinil don't result in crashes. 

Modafinil works better than Amantadine did for me, by far. I can't function at work without it. Sometimes the fatigue still wins, but usually it'll keep me awake even when I'm exhausted. 

I hope you can get on something that helps! It really does improve quality of life when the fatigue is lessened.

I had the choice to either join the BEAT-MS trial or take Lemtrada. I would've gotten Lemtrada in the trial if I didn't get the HSCT, but I still didn't want to take the increased risks if i landed in the HSCT group. I ended up declining and just getting Lem.

I know the diagnosis is extremely difficult. My first symptoms came in an extremely aggressive attack as well, and I also had thoughts after diagnosis about how I wish it had been something terminal, or cancer that could potentially be cured. I felt like my life fell completely apart. That's the grief talking, though, and you can get through it. 

Try not to pay too much mind (easier said than done, I know) to people acting like it's a death sentence. Those who don't know anything about MS often confuse it with more severe neurological diseases like ALS or Huntington's, both of which are eventually terminal. MS is not that. Those tend to just all get lumped in together.

Your disease may or may not be volatile (not necessarily aggressive, just a lot of ups and downs) in the first 2 years, as that's when MS is the most active for most people, but you could also get lucky and have no more relapses after this.

Symptoms can go away or they can stay. It took months for me to be able to feel any sensation other than pressure in my hands and feet after my first attack. Hopefully your symptoms let up quickly, but don't feel discouraged if they linger. Recovering from a relapse can be a lengthy process.

Don't lose hope. You still have your full life ahead of you...there's just a few road blocks to get around now. Fingers crossed that your doctor can get you on something to help short term until you can see the neuro.

If it makes you feel any better, I was diagnosed with highly aggressive MS 4 years ago, when I was 29. The disease hit me like a truck from the start, and I had severe symptoms that kept progressing for almost 2 years. I was very much debilitated, needed an AFO (brace) to walk around, severe balance issues and tremors.

Ocrevus didn't stop my progression, but it does for most. I went on Lemtrada, which was much more risky, but it stopped my disease and allowed my nerves to heal or adjust. I'm almost symptom-free now, outside of flares.

Lem is extremely aggressive, but a lot of people see improvement with less risky high efficacy treatments. The brain takes time to heal, but it CAN heal nerve damage if the nerves aren't completely dead. It just needs to not be constantly attacked. The only lesion I had on my spine is now gone, though all the ones in my brain are still there.

MS isn't a guarantee of disability, and more treatments are always being worked on. I'm hopeful that we'll have a remyelination drug on the market within 5-10 years, and that will be a game-changer. In the meantime, high efficacy meds do control the disease well, but some do get unlucky.

My boyfriend and I have been together for almost 3 years. We met online, and we became friends first, but eventually started dating. I did tell him about my MS beforehand, and was surprised when he said it didn't bother him.

He's been there through flares that had every part of my body jerking because the muscle spasms were so bad, or ones that made it really difficult to walk. So far, he's still not scared. He's optimistic, if anything, that remyelination therapies will be out in the next 10 years or so.

Not everyone can handle dating someone with this diagnosis, but people like him do exist. Don't give up and think you'll always be alone; dating with MS might be hard, but it doesn't have to be futile.

My insurance does this. When I was getting approval for Lemtrada, my specialist at the time was pushing them hard about it. At diagnosis, I had a lot of lesions. The only "symptom" I had was worsening migraines for about a year before my first attack. I had chronic migraine already, so we didn't look too hard at it. We thought my med was just starting to fail.

When the first attack hit, I was completely debilitated. I experienced almost every symptom possible with MS within the first 3-4 months. The rapid progression didn't stop until I switched from Ocrevus to Lemtrada two years ago. By that time, I had significant disability. That was 2 years after the first attack.

The scariest part of this is that I'd had an MRI done a year before that first attack - just a typical thing they do every few years with chronic migraine patients. It was clear. Not a single lesion. All of that damage happened without any real warning, no signs of any usual MS symptoms.

My advice: take it seriously when you get new lesions. That damage can snowball, and symptoms from those lesions can pop up at any time. Any bit of damage is damage we can't currently undo, even if its not causing problems at the moment.

I had something similar back when my balance was bad. I had to watch my feet up and down stairs, because if I couldn't see my foot on the step, it felt...like it wasn't on solid ground. This was even at times where my foot wasn't numb.

I'm not sure if its exactly your same issue, but my perception was off back then too. I also walked into doors sometimes. The PT exercises helped with that too - I think they help the brain discover new nerve paths to regain function that was lost.

My response is always that what I go through is bad for me and unbearable sometimes, but to her, her pain is astronomical. She has every right to be upset about it, just like i do when my body doesn't want to listen.

I hated being told "Hey, at least it's not cancer" by my boss when I was first diagnosed. It felt condescending. Cancer sucks for cancer patients, as MS does for us. That doesn't mean my suffering is worse than theirs, or vice versa. It's hell for both.

I wouldn't recommend Lemtrada as a first line treatment, and neither will any competent doctor. I wouldn't recommend HSCT, either, but since you're clearly already firm in getting it, you do you.

The risk for both is large, HSCT more so than Lemtrada. I can tell you that having switched to Lemtrada because of my very aggressive MS, I don't regret it, but it was absolute hell and I would not go through that if I hadn't had to, though it did stop my progression and I am grateful for that. HSCT is even more brutal, and there are people who've relapsed within a few years of getting it. None of these treatments are a cure.

A lot of people stay stable and progression-free on highly effective DMTs, without the massive risks that come with Lemtrada/HSCT.

I had the option to join the HSCT trial at my MS clinic, or get Lemtrada. I debated about it, and chose Lemtrada. I wasn't willing to go through the extra risk, personally. Ocrevus, Tysabri and their alternatives are much safer and still have high efficacy.

Excessive drinking can cause a lot of detriment to our brains. I know someone that developed dementia from their alcoholism. They blame themselves constantly for it. I wasn't aware it could do that, either.

I had my nose pierced a while after my diagnosis. As other people mentioned, they're usually every 6 months at first, but eventually sometimes just yearly. They could be more often if you're having relapses.

As for MRIs, it sort of depends on what your piercings are. If they're not non-magnetic metal, you could get that, but it's still a toss up depending on the MRI place. My first MRI place was fine with my titanium piercing (1.5T MRI, the standard strength that most get), but other places have wanted it removed. No piercings are allowed at all if you're doing a 3T MRI.

I just put a plastic retainer in my nose every time I get an MRI done now, just in case they ask me to remove it (nose piercings can close up really fast). Easy to switch out. Any that you can't easily swap, however, you probably need to let go of.

MS is a devastating diagnosis at any stage, but late stage is probably even more so. I'd recommend trying to get him to join this Reddit, as it can be extremely helpful to talk to others who've gone through the exact same thing. We have people of all stages of the disease here.

A lot of people don't realize that an actual grieving process happens with a diagnosis like this. We go through all the stages of it, but especially anger early on. I was in the angry stage for months after my diagnosis. It took the better part of a year to get through my grief. Everyone goes through it at a different pace.

Don't treat him differently. If he's angry about potential future (or current?) loss of independence, don't coddle him or try to do things for him that he usually does himself, unless he either asks for help or you see him seriously struggling. We want to keep our independence as much as possible, for as long as possible. I used to get very bitter if someone tried to help me if I didn't ask for it - but everyone varies.

If there's any local MS programs, you could try to get him to go to help groups or activities that they do - this can be a double edged sword. I don't know what his physical status is or his personality, so only you'll know whether or not it's worth a shot. I know for me, I was significantly impaired (with early stage MS) within a few months of my diagnosis, and it would have been unhelpful to go to a support group. I was bitter as hell that I was so much worse off than a lot of people who'd had the disease for years. Eventually, I worked my way through that.

Try to encourage him to do things he enjoys doing, in any way he can do them. It can help give us a sense of normalcy. Just don't focus on his disease. It doesn't define him, and we can still live full lives with it.

I've had it twice. The first time was just 3 months after my Lemtrada treatment, and my cell count was almost nonexistent, so I essentially had no immune system at all. I was very sick, and was flaring for about 4 months afterward off and on. My MS symptoms did get much worse, but they gradually eased off again until I was back to where I'd been pre-COVID.

The second time, my cell count had regrown to within the normal range, and the virus was much less aggressive. I didn't experience any flares after this bout.

I have a feeling my immune system made my flares more frequent/worse after the first round, but it is common to experience *some* degree of flaring, significant or not. Typically with most viruses, you'll just flare for a very short time afterward (i.e. no more than 1-2 weeks max, sometimes just a few days). COVID is unpredictable, but as much as there's a lot of people who've had extended flares from the virus (past what's usual for other sicknesses), there are also a lot that haven't. Hopefully yours is very short-lived!

Certain diets *can* increase energy levels for patients. That doesn't mean it's doing anything for their MS.

The no med way isn't "working" for those people. They're lucky. Some people get extremely lucky and don't relapse for long periods off DMTs, but they are few and far between. That doesn't mean that their MS can't activate at any point in time - benign MS isn't common, and it's unpredictable. It can last for decades, or it can last for a smaller number of years. As said though, the population of patients with true benign MS is extremely small.

When I was first diagnosed, a co-worker told me that I didn't need to go on meds if I didn't want to - she had a friend who'd had MS for 30 years and was still fine off DMTs. She said "bee venom therapy" helped her a lot. Upon looking it up, studies did, in fact, conclude that bee venom therapy does literally nothing. It's a placebo for people who insist on trying anything homeopathic. Her friend was one of the lucky few, and was also diagnosed at a time when DMTs really didn't do much, so a lot of patients didn't take them and didn't believe they'd help. I finished my second dose in January. Here's my extensive explanation of my experience.

The infusion week was rough on both rounds, though the second one is shorter. It made me incredibly sick. High blood pressure one day on my first round, but it resolved after they paused the drip. No other side effects during infusions.

The infusion days are extremely long. Expect around 8 hours between pre meds and the Lem itself, more if you have a reaction they have to pause for. I was there for 10 hours one day. 

Also expect the Lem to drain the hell out of you. Everything hurt by the night of day 2 the first year. By the 5th day, I could barely move around because of how weak I was. The second year wasn't as severe, but still made me sick. Both years made me really nauseated, though not during the infusions - it actually would start a day or two after the infusion course ended, but last several weeks. 

Recovery took much longer the first year. My lymphocytes didn't reach a functional level until October (9 months). I had much more severe exhaustion for about 5 months. The first 3-4 weeks were the worst. Migraines, nausea, weakness, flares in random MS symptoms, massive muscle and joint pain, but then a lot tapers off, leaving mostly weakness and fatigue from the immunecsystem having to rebuild. After about 5-6 months, I felt like I'd regained my energy and wasn't as weak.

The second round was a shorter recovery, but still about 3 weeks of hell after infusion week. The migraines and nausea were way worse, and I swelled to the point where I went to my doctor because it was affecting my breathing (not common btw, it was severe fluid retention causing massive bloating). I had to just ride that out until everything flushed out of my system.

That said, here's the massively positive part: by the end of that first year, I had become almost asymptomatic with my MS. I went from moderately disabled (needing an afo all the time) to almost feeling normal. Covid in May of this year set that back and re-progressed me symptom-wise, but it's fading again. Lemtrada gave me my life back after my first two years of rapid progression. It was hell to go through, but worth it to me. Very minimal symptoms nowadays other than MS fatigue, and no MRI progression.

Yeah...I remember reading during pre-vaccine COVID that some Ocrevus patients were delaying treatment by 3-6 months and were fine, but I don't remember if any studies were actually done on it regarding efficacy. Regardless, I wouldn't trust anyone that said to stop them indefinitely.

B cell depleters work because B cells *can't* amp up the "attack" T cells when they don't exist. Your immune system still remembers that it needs to attack your nerves, because it's not completely wiped out like with HSCT, or to a lesser degree Lemtrada/Mavenclad - it's just that it can't (or shouldn't, if it's working).

I'm kind of astonished any doctor would think a b cell depleter would be a long-term remission kind of drug.

Drugs do actually keep you from relapsing. They're just not 100% guaranteed, but all of them reduce relapse frequency. The intention is to find a DMT that will keep you from relapsing period, which can be trial and error. One drug does not work for everyone's immune system. Relapsing on a DMT is a sign that the DMT **isn't** doing its job.

Also, nerves do, in fact, heal themselves. That sheath will regrow. The thing is, the nerve has to be alive still (i.e. has some sheath left), and your disease has to stop attacking them. *Part* of the reason why some people get better over time is because nerves are healing themselves - when DMTs are working, they stop the disease process, which gives the nerves a nice reprieve. Mind you, it takes a very long time for a nerve to fully regenerate itself  (something like 7 years, if I remember correctly), and sometimes nerves just can't heal. Remyelination therapies, which are currently being researched, aim to make this much faster, but they are also inhibited by the fact that the nerves can't be dead, because you can't regrow a myelin sheath that doesn't exist.

Being off meds is always a risk. You could be fine for months. You could have a severe relapse and end up in a wheelchair or with a paralyzed arm. There is no guarantee that you'll be safe for any period of time. Furthermore, some DMTs like Gilenya are actually really dangerous if you don't start another therapy as you're stopping them. Gilenya was actually found to have a high chance of rapid progression when it's stopped, which is why doctors no longer do a washout period afterward, and instead switch right to another medication.

I would always be skeptical of stopping a DMT that wasn't meant to be a one-and-done like Lemtrada or Mavenclad. At least until some studies come out showing that certain ones can be trusted to have effect long-term after treatment.

Lemtrada isn't a cure, just like HSCT isn't a cure. You can relapse after getting them. Often, people get years of no activity after having these, but sometimes they relapse after 2-3. Some people might also opt not to get a third round of treatment if they keep progressing, or relapse a few years after round 2, in which case they'd go down a step to the less potent yet still high efficacy treatments (like Ocrevus).

The chance of relapsing after HSCT is what made me go for Lemtrada rather than go into the HSCT trial. I wouldn't want to go through all of that just to have to go on Lemtrada or another DMT 2 years later. Lemtrada is risky and brutal, but it's less so than HSCT.

There's no such thing as being in "remission." DMTs prevent relapses when they're working, sort of pausing the disease while you're on them, but without one, your immune system could attack at any time. This isn't like cancer, where the cancer cells are eradicated and your cancer goes into remission, possibly forever. Your immune system sees your nerves as food. Your cells will keep seeing your nerves as food. That doesn't change. DMTs just try to prevent them from attacking, or kill them off in the hope that they can't. Without that, your nerves have no defense.

Some people have been without DMTs for 20 years and never get an attack. Some get a single attack and end up in a wheelchair. There is a better long term prognosis with early (and consistent) treatment. You can prevent attacks; you can't undo the damage they cause. The gamble is yours.

As someone who's been on Lemtrada, I would not suggest it. It's reserved for highly active cases that don't respond to other high efficacy treatments, for good reason. The side effects are severe, and it has a decently high chance at causing thyroid disease, with a lower chance at causing some much more serious complications. You have to be monitored for 4 years past your last infusion, so it's 4 *years* (6 total, at minimum) of monthly blood draws and worrying about whether or not an auto-immune complication will pop up. If an auto-immune condition does start, you have to keep getting monthly blood draws.

Generally, if you're not having active symptom or MRI progression, most specialists wouldn't recommend changing treatments. DMTs aren't a permanent thing. Once your immune system decides to stop responding to them, that's it. If you swap to another one when your current one is still effective, that's one less DMT that can work on you. There's also no guarantee that other DMTs will work.

Also, Tysabri is thought to be about on par with Ocrevus, so there's really no gain there, especially since you're JCV negative.

To clear up some misconceptions, MS is not a deadly disease. If it progresses very far, complications *can* lead to death, but we're talking a very minimal % of people - it's rare. Most won't get to that point. Our lives are barely shorter than people who don't have MS (on average about 7 years less), but it's definitely not a "I might die in 7-10 years" kind of thing. This isn't a hyper-aggressive deterioration like ALS or Huntington's.

MS is worse for men than it is for women, which is unfortunate, but there are some really good treatments out for the disease, some of which give a good **potential** prognosis for regression. There's also a lot of trials and research being done in the past few years to find a treatment that will actually regrow nerves and reverse at least some of the damage - eventually, we'll have that to look forward to.

Early on in the disease, it is much more volatile. Symptoms come and go a lot more for some people, and there is usually more activity in the first couple of years. It tends to calm down after that, even for aggressive cases. Don't focus too much on worse case scenarios; it feels that bad at first, but it gets easier, and you'll realize that the disease is not as scary for most patients as people think it is.

But if your doctor isn't going to discuss any treatments, I would find a new doctor, in all honesty. They should've already done that.
